newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK's Patten takes aim at his post-97 successor.
newsitem.headline: HK's Patten takes aim at his post-97 successor.

text.p: Hong Kong Governor Chris Patten on Saturday criticised his likely successor after the British colony reverts to China next year for suggesting the Democratic Party had no role to play in the territory after the handover.

"You can't, nobody can, simply freeze out of the political debate in Hong Kong, out of the dialogue about Hong Kong's future, those who represent majority opinion in Hong Kong," Patten told Hong Kong government radio during a visit to Japan.

"I don't think you can govern any community against the grain of public opinion...People want a say in decisions made about their future and quite right too. That's the aspiration the Democrats represent and that's not going to go away," he said.

Shipping tycoon Tung Chee-hwa, tipped as the territory's post-colonial leader, said on Wednesday the Democratic Party, Hong Kong's largest, must stop confronting China if it wanted to participate in Hong Kong's political establishment after the 1997 handover.
China has branded the Democratic Party, vocal critics of Chinese policies, as "subversive" and barred the party from committees now shaping post-colonial political structures.
More than 150 years of colonial rule will end at midnight next June 30 when Britiain hands Hong Kong back to China.

Besides Tung, former Hong Kong Chief Justice Yang Ti Liang and businessman Peter Woo are running for the post of chief executive, which will be chosen by a China-controlled 400-strong Selection Committee on December 11.
Tung is expected to win the contest as he took 206 votes in a first round ballot two weeks ago, compared with Yang's 82 and Woo's 54 votes.
